01 Wunderman · 2016 · Dannon · CPG

Activia

“It’s Within You”
The insight The key to success is turning your internal critic into your best ally.

Situation

The brief was to make Activia a purpose-driven brand in the US. The existing ladder ran Bifidus Regularis → experts in digestive health → reduces bloating, gas, discomfort and rumbling → feeling good starts from the inside. Clinical, functional, and impossible for a younger woman to care about.

What I did

Original qualitative interviews plus a large-scale quantitative study, run before the positioning was written. The number that changed the work: 80% of US women said they were the biggest obstacle to achieving their own goals. Culture tells us to silence our external critics; the one actually holding us back is internal.

What happened

The ladder was rebuilt to an emotional end benefit — positive and empowered to navigate life — and the idea came out of the brand’s own language: “It’s Within You.” Co-led the repositioning and the pitch that won it.

02 Zeno Group · 2022 · New business win

Dremel

“You Got This”
The insight Gen Z is the “I don’t know how to do it, but if I watch enough YouTube I can figure it out” generation.

Situation

Cheaper competitor brands were flooding the market. Dremel needed to stop competing on specs and make an emotional connection — with a customer the rotary tool category had never spoken to. DIY marketing still assumed a man in a garage.

What I did

Led the strategic workshop that won the business, then owned the arc: audience research, segmentation, findings, client presentation, handoff to creative. Internal framework “Make it Yours.” The target became the “new DIYer” — first-timers at the front of a new chapter, and the work follows them from a college dorm to an apartment to a first house rather than assuming the suburban garage.

What happened

“You Got This” launched April 2022 — three spots (“Tub,” “Mirror,” “New Place”) across digital and social. 120M+ media impressions, 430K+ clicks across five platforms, 2K+ earned media and press placements, and 85.5K product category page views on Dremel.com.

03 Zeno Group · 2021–2023 · Agency of record

Lenovo

“Work for Humankind”
The insight The person who feels the broken workflow isn’t the person who signs for the fix — so sell to the sufferer and let them argue upward.

Situation

Agency-of-record work at tens of millions in annual fees, with separate research budgets for positioning and launches. Lenovo needed a distinctive voice in the remote-work conversation — one that reached millennials and Gen Z rather than restating a spec story to IT buyers.

What I did

Ran 15–20 in-depth interviews with Lenovo stakeholders and executives across roles, which surfaced the one claim only Lenovo could make: a genuinely connected stack — cloud, AI, systems and professional hardware together. Then inverted the target — away from the person signing the purchase order, toward the person living the broken workflow. Account research also found 86% believed remote work should be used to support local communities.

What happened

Work for Humankind invited people to work remotely from Robinson Crusoe Island, 350 miles off Chile, while supporting conservation — Lenovo built a tech hub and took a 900-person community from 1 Mbps to 200 Mbps. 4,500 applied; volunteers gave over 1,000 hours. 2,038 pieces of earned coverage and 3.6 billion impressions, 295.8M paid impressions, 13.3M video views, and a 76% year-over-year rise in Lenovo thought-leadership articles. Shorty Awards: Silver Honor for Creative Use of Technology, and a Global Campaign finalist.

04 Ogilvy · 2019–2021 · Enterprise technology

IBM

“Let’s Put Smart to Work”
The insight IBM was invisible and everywhere at once — behind the technologies people touched daily without ever seeing the name.

Situation

IBM’s best proof lived in dense technical case studies — real work in AI, cloud and blockchain, written for engineers and buyers. A general audience had no way in, and no reason to care about enterprise infrastructure.

What I did

Took those complex case studies and decoded them into human stories — the person, the problem, what changed — without flattening the technology underneath. Those stories became the brief for “Dear Tech,” the anthem film for “Let’s Put Smart to Work.”

What happened

Owned the digital experiences and website where people could discover and play with the stories of what IBM was actually making smarter — interactive rather than explanatory, so the proof did the persuading.

05 McGarryBowen · Consumer technology

Intel

“Experience Amazing”
The insight Millennials don’t buy the processor. They buy the afternoon it makes possible.

Situation

Intel sold itself the way chipmakers always had — gigahertz, cores, nanometers — to a generation that had stopped reading spec sheets. The brand needed to become tangible to younger consumers rather than merely present in their laptops.

What I did

Uncovered the winning insight behind the campaign: millennials value experiences over technology. The processor is a means; what it makes possible is the product. That reframe moved Intel’s argument off the silicon and onto the life around it.

What happened

It let Intel keep its single most valuable asset — the word Inside — while changing what was inside from a chip to an experience. The work ran as “Experience What’s Inside” and “Experience Amazing,” fronted by Jim Parsons across a long run of spots, showing Intel through prosthetics, NASA, sport, gaming and music instead of performance claims.

06 Zeno Group · 2022–2023 · Procter & Gamble

Zevo

“Bugxiety”
The insight Nobody buys pest control because of efficacy. They buy it because of the half-second when something flies at your face.

Situation

Every brand in the category competes on kill rate, and Zevo had a genuinely different product — UV light traps and essential-oil sprays rather than harsh chemicals. But the purchase isn’t rational. It’s dread, and nobody had named it.

What I did

Wrote the positioning and the creative brief around a coined feeling: bugxiety. Built a two-season architecture on top of it — summer peak bug season, then holiday and winter critter prevention — across the Flying Insect Trap and the plant-derived Multi-Insect spray.

What happened

Briefed the creative agency, Curiosity, who built the platform from it. Work at this scale takes time — the campaign went live in summer 2023 with Rebel Wilson, months after I’d left Zeno, and a holiday flight followed that December — the second season of the architecture, on air. That spring, a national Maru survey of 1,066 Americans put a number on the feeling the brief had already named: 71% report bugxiety, and more rate their anxiety about bugs (46%) than about getting fired (44%).

07 Wunderman · 2016 · Dannon · CPG

Danimals

“Imagination Is Everything”
The insight Excitement lives in possibility — in our imagination. Routine is where it goes to die.

Situation

The ask was an emotional connection with children in the grocery aisle. But the brand was talking to two people at once: kids got exciting taste, parents got healthy routine — and those two benefits were quietly cancelling each other out.

What I did

Named the problem precisely: when Danimals’ exciting taste becomes part of mom’s healthy routine, it stops being exciting and becomes boring. Kids love the unexpected and hate the expected. So the challenge wasn’t awareness — it was make routine exciting again.

What happened

Yogurt is versatile, malleable, adaptable — a blank canvas. Cereal dressing, frosting, a pool for Goldfish to swim in; a companion on safari, a career as a firefighter. The brand’s job became to own imagination, with Bongo recast from mascot to guide, and reasons to believe built separately for the kid and for mom.

08 Wunderman · Nonprofit · Adoption

Boroughbreds

Animal Care Centers of NYC
The insight New Yorkers are a different breed. So are the animals that come from here.

Situation

Shelter adoption marketing runs on pity, and pity is a weak motivator. ACC’s animals were being read as damaged goods next to purebreds with papers — in a city of eight million people, most of them unaware the animals were waiting at all.

What I did

Invented a breed. Every New Yorker has their own story, their own lineage, their own look, and an unreasonable devotion to the city — and so does every animal that comes out of it. A Boroughbred is a mash-up of NYC neighborhoods and breeds, which turns “mixed” from a defect into a pedigree.

What happened

In ACC’s words, not just a campaign but a movement. Billboards in Times Square and across the city, the adoption site rebuilt around searching for your own Boroughbred, plus branded doggie bags, discounted rides to the shelters, social takeovers run by the animals, and scent-infused ads placed low to the ground for dogs. ACC closed 2017 with a placement rate over 90% and 21,848 animals placed.

09 Wunderman · 2017 · Animal health

Zoetis

Vision and mission, Companion Animal Division
The insight “I think we are so much more than our products. We just aren’t communicating what that is yet.”

Situation

A house of products with no shared sentence to say about itself. In the division’s own words: “because there is such a diverse group of products, everyone is kind of siloed.” A vision and mission had to do four jobs — unify, act as north star, inspire pride, and improve everyday decisions.

What I did

Built the workshop on evidence rather than opinion: internal interviews, veterinarian interviews and social listening. Vets wanted four things — set a high standard for care, make care more accessible, share expertise credibly, and express real commitment. One put the stakes plainly: “veterinary medicine has become a service for the wealthy.”

What happened

Facilitated the session around four drafted possibilities — framed by world, relationship and health — from “to progress humanity through our pets” to “to invigorate the human spirit by strengthening the pet-owner bond.” The room chose; the research made choosing possible. That workshop became the foundation for the Zoetis Petcare campaign, which I helped create — built on the idea that pets take care of us.
